Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":6.838,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

{"query":"link saturated utilization shift traffic routing metric change without change log","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.914,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":4.518,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":2.411,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"},{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.135,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"}]}

{"query":"link utilization drops to zero while latency stays normal, traffic shifted to alternate path, routing metric","results":[{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":5.787,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.832,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":5.337,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

{"query":"link down interface status polling probe missing counters absent","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":8.974,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":7.039,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"link down vs routing metric change traffic shift to alternate link, probe fail","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.477,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":3.46,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.

{"query":"link down vs routing metric drain traffic shifted to zero utilization","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.399,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":4.027,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

{"query":"pop unreachable NMS poll missing telemetry gap no data link","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":6.043,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.467,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

{"query":"link_no_data telemetry gap with svc_unreachable probe failure, distinguish collector blanking from real outage","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":8.131,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":6.272,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"demand surge vs routing misconfiguration traffic shift between links","results":[{"runbook":"RB06_demand_surge","score":4.335,"text":"# RB06 Demand surge at a PoP

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":3.055,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Fault type: demand_surge. Root: a PoP (the source of the extra traffic).

Symptoms:
- Utilisation rises together on several links attached to one PoP, ramping up over some steps rather than jumping.
- Downstream links on paths from that PoP may hit high utilisation (link_util_high) and start to discard.
- Latency and loss rise on services from that PoP once links congest.

Checks:
- Do the busiest links share one end router? The shared router is the root, not the busiest single link.
- Is the rise larger than the normal daily pattern? Compare with the same window one day earlier.
- A drain in the change log also raises utilisation on neighbouring links; check that first.

Action: identify the traffic source; apply rate limits or add capacity; reroute where possible.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":4.092,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":3.66,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

{"query":"planned drain routing metric traffic shift utilization drop neighbour link","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":3.986,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":3.742,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

Symptoms:

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

{"query":"planned link outage maintenance window services unreachable versus link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.077,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":4.539,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"}]}

Applies to: every incident. Fault types: all.

1. Read the alert list for the window. Group alerts by element. Service alerts (svc_loss_sla, svc_latency_sla, svc_unreachable) are symptoms seen at the edge; link and router alerts point closer to the cause.
2. Check the change log before anything else. A planned drain, outage or other change on an element in or just before the window explains alerts on that element and on links that took its rerouted traffic.
3. For each candidate element, look at its telemetry in the window against the same window one day earlier. A real fault changes something that was normal the day before.
4. Use the topology: a single root usually explains several symptoms. Find the element shared by the paths of the alerted services (shared elements), and check its neighbours.
5. Decide between: a fault (name the root element and type), planned maintenance only, or no fault. Do not report a fault when every symptom is explained by a logged change.
6. Evidence must quote element ids and values exactly as the tools returned them.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":3.257,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.

{"query":"planned outage link down service unreachable alert expected","results":[{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":4.2,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":4.118,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

{"query":"planned outage link no telemetry traffic reroute loss alert","results":[{"runbook":"RB01_triage","score":3.725,"text":"# RB01 Incident triage (general)

Applies to: every incident. Fault types: all.

1. Read the alert list for the window. Group alerts by element. Service alerts (svc_loss_sla, svc_latency_sla, svc_unreachable) are symptoms seen at the edge; link and router alerts point closer to the cause.
2. Check the change log before anything else. A planned drain, outage or other change on an element in or just before the window explains alerts on that element and on links that took its rerouted traffic.
3. For each candidate element, look at its telemetry in the window against the same window one day earlier. A real fault changes something that was normal the day before.
4. Use the topology: a single root usually explains several symptoms. Find the element shared by the paths of the alerted services (shared elements), and check its neighbours.
5. Decide between: a fault (name the root element and type), planned maintenance only, or no fault. Do not report a fault when every symptom is explained by a logged change.
6. Evidence must quote element ids and values exactly as the tools returned them.
"},{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":3.652,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.

Applies to: every incident. Fault types: all.

1. Read the alert list for the window. Group alerts by element. Service alerts (svc_loss_sla, svc_latency_sla, svc_unreachable) are symptoms seen at the edge; link and router alerts point closer to the cause.
2. Check the change log before anything else. A planned drain, outage or other change on an element in or just before the window explains alerts on that element and on links that took its rerouted traffic.
3. For each candidate element, look at its telemetry in the window against the same window one day earlier. A real fault changes something that was normal the day before.
4. Use the topology: a single root usually explains several symptoms. Find the element shared by the paths of the alerted services (shared elements), and check its neighbours.

"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":3.821,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.

"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.139,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.

{"query":"link utilisation drops to zero but probes still succeed; routing metric change vs link down","results":[{"runbook":"RB05_link_degradation","score":6.269,"text":"# RB05 Link degradation (loss or latency)

Fault type: link_degradation. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The link stays up, but its one-hop latency rises (link_latency_high) or it drops packets (link_discards).
- Services crossing the link breach latency or loss SLAs; services not crossing it are fine.
- Utilisation is often unchanged, because routing does not move traffic away from a degraded but up link.

Checks:
- Compare the link's latency and discards with the same window one day earlier.
- Find the element shared by the paths of the services with SLA alerts; a degraded link is usually on all of them.
- Small degradations may raise no alert: look at the telemetry of links on the shared paths even without alerts.

Action: raise with the transmission team; consider moving traffic off the link with a metric change.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":5.617,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"}]}

Symptoms:

{"query":"planned drain routing metric raised traffic leaves link expected loss during drain","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":10.415,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":6.376,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.

{"query":"link no data telemetry missing vs link down vs node down leaf PoP","results":[{"runbook":"RB09_telemetry_gaps","score":5.965,"text":"# RB09 Telemetry gaps and collector problems (general)

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.603,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"planned outage link down services unreachable after maintenance window","results":[{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":6.764,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"},{"runbook":"RB03_node_down","score":4.449,"text":"# RB03 Router (PoP) down

Fault type: node_down. Root: a PoP (router).

Symptoms:
- The router stops answering polls (pop_unreachable) when status polling exists.
- Every link attached to the router goes dark or reads zero at the same time.
- Services that start or end at the PoP become unreachable; services that transited it reroute.

Checks:
- Do all links of one PoP show the same outage at the same step? A single dark link is a link fault; all links of one router is the router.
- Is there a planned outage on the PoP in the change log?

Action: dispatch to the site; check power and control plane; confirm traffic has moved to alternate paths.
"}]}

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.
"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":5.202,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
"}]}

{"query":"planned traffic drain routing metric raised link utilization expected","results":[{"runbook":"RB07_routing_misconfig","score":5.804,"text":"# RB07 Routing misconfiguration (link metric change)

Fault type: routing_misconfig. Root: the link whose routing metric was changed.

Symptoms:
- Traffic moves suddenly at one step: utilisation drops on one link and rises on others (metric raised), or rises sharply on one link (metric lowered, pulling traffic onto it).
- No interface goes down. Service latency changes because paths changed.
- Unlike a drain, there is no matching entry in the change log.

Checks:
- Look for a step change in utilisation on one link with no outage and no logged change.
- If a link lost most of its traffic while staying up, and nothing is logged, the metric on that link is the likely root.
- If one link suddenly carries much more than the day before, check whether paths were pulled onto it.

Action: compare the running routing metric with the intended configuration; roll back the change.
"},{"runbook":"RB08_maintenance_and_drains","score":5.511,"text":"# RB08 Planned maintenance and drains (general)

Applies to: incidents that overlap a change-log entry.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.
- A no-op entry is logged work that did not touch traffic.
- During and just after a change window, alerts on the changed element and on links that took its traffic are expected.

How to decide:
- If every alerted element is the changed element or carries its rerouted traffic, and nothing else is abnormal, the answer is planned maintenance, not a fault.
- A fault can still happen during maintenance: look for symptoms on elements the change does not explain.
- Do not blame the changed element for symptoms that started before the change window.
"}]}

Applies to: alerts of type link_no_data or link_probe_fail, and missing values in series.

- Missing telemetry is not a fault by itself. Collectors drop data for single links or for every link of one router for a few steps.
- A down link also stops reporting. Tell them apart:
  - A collector gap is usually short and often hits several unrelated links or a whole router at once, while services crossing them are fine.
  - When a link goes down, its traffic moves to neighbours (their utilisation rises), and services crossing it see loss at the start.
- A missing one-hop latency probe while counters still report means the probe failed, not the link.
- When status polling is not available, telemetry absence plus traffic moving to neighbours is the main evidence of an outage.

- A drain raises the routing metric of a link so traffic leaves it before work starts. The drained link's utilisation falls; neighbours carry more. Latency on rerouted services can rise. Nothing is broken.
- A planned outage ("down") takes a link or router down on purpose. Telemetry on it stops or reads zero, exactly as in a real failure, and status alerts fire.

"},{"runbook":"RB02_link_down","score":4.214,"text":"# RB02 Link down

Fault type: link_down. Root: a link.

Symptoms:
- The interface is reported down (link_status_down) when status polling exists.
- Telemetry on the link stops or reads zero: utilisation at 0 with the one-hop latency probe missing, or no data at all when status events are not available.
- Short loss on services that crossed the link while routing converges, then latency changes on the services that were rerouted.
- Neighbouring links (sharing a router) pick up the traffic: utilisation rises on them.

Checks:
- Is there a planned outage ("down") or drain on this link in the change log? If so it is maintenance, not a fault.
- Are many links blanked at the same time? That points to a collector gap (see RB09), not a link failure.

Action: open a fault ticket with the carrier or field team for the link; confirm rerouting has capacity.
